hints: Look closely at the last word in each option. Is one triple helix on its own a fibre, or is a fibre made from many triple helices grouped together?
Remember the special amino acid pattern that lets the three chains pack so tightly, and check if the single chains are true alpha-helices like in other proteins.
walkthrough:
**Separate molecule from fibre**

Think small to large. Three polypeptide chains wind together to make one collagen molecule, also called tropocollagen. Many of these molecules then pack together to make a much thicker collagen fibre. So any option that calls one triple helix a fibre is mixing up two levels.

**Check the shape of the single chains**

The individual collagen chains are helical, but they are not alpha-helices. They form a looser left-handed helix with a repeating sequence, quite different from the classic coiled alpha-helix stabilised by internal hydrogen bonds. So we must reject any option that calls them alpha-helices.

**Add the glycine rule**

The key to tight packing is that every third amino acid is glycine, the smallest amino acid. Its tiny R group (just H) fits in the centre of the triple helix where there is no room for larger side chains. The complete correct description must include this, plus the idea that many triple helices form a fibre.

options.A: Correct about three helical chains, but wrong to call the single triple helix a fibre. A fibre is made of many triple-helix molecules packed together.
options.B: Wrong because the single chains are not alpha-helices. The second sentence about many triple helices binding as a fibre is true, but the alpha-helix error makes the whole option incorrect.
options.C: Wrong to call the triple helix a fibre, and it also leaves out the essential every-third-glycine detail needed for tight winding.
options.D: Fully correct. It states the glycine every third residue pattern, the tight triple helix molecule, and that many such helices group to form a fibre.
